title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
book: NCERT India and the Contemporary World – II
subject: history
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (History: 18 marks + 2 map marks; there is no map item from this chapter).

blocks.title: A painting that imagined the future
blocks.body:
In 1848 a French artist, **Frédéric Sorrieu**, made a set of four prints showing his dream of a world of **"democratic and social republics"**. In the first print, the peoples of Europe and America, men and women of all ages, march in a long line and offer homage to the **Statue of Liberty**, who holds the torch of Enlightenment in one hand and the Charter of the Rights of Man in the other. In the foreground lie the shattered remains of the symbols of **absolutist institutions**. Above them, Christ, saints and angels watch: a sign of fraternity among the nations.

In 1848 this was only a dream: Europe was ruled by kings and emperors over many small states and huge mixed empires. By 1871 Germany and Italy had become nation-states. How did this happen? That is the story of this chapter.

blocks.title: The general with the red shirts
blocks.body:
Garibaldi was a sailor from Nice who joined Mazzini's Young Italy movement and was sentenced to death after a failed rising in 1834. He escaped to South America and returned to fight for Italy.

In 1860 he led his famous **Expedition of the Thousand**, armed volunteers in red shirts, into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, drove out the Spanish Bourbon rulers and handed the south over to King Victor Emmanuel II. Ordinary people with courage and a shared idea helped create a nation.
blocks.future: History builds the skills of reading sources, weighing evidence and arguing a case: useful in civil services, law, journalism, teaching, archives and museums.

blocks.question: Before 1800, people in Europe mostly saw themselves as subjects of a king or members of a local community. What new idea made them feel they belonged to one **nation**?
options: A shared identity: common language, history, culture and equal rights as citizens
Paying taxes to the same king
blocks.explanation: A nation is held together by a sense of shared identity and history. The French Revolution turned subjects into citizens, and this idea spread across Europe.

sections.title: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation

blocks.title: From subjects to citizens
blocks.body:
The first clear expression of nationalism came with the **French Revolution of 1789**. Political and constitutional changes transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of French citizens: **the people** would now form the nation and shape its destiny.

**Measures to create a collective identity among the French people:**
- The ideas of ***la patrie*** (the fatherland) and ***le citoyen*** (the citizen) stressed a united community with equal rights under a constitution.
- A new French flag, the **tricolour**, replaced the royal standard.
- The Estates General was elected by active citizens and renamed the **National Assembly**.
- New hymns were composed, oaths taken and martyrs commemorated, all in the name of the nation.
- A **centralised administrative system** made uniform laws for all citizens.
- Internal customs duties and dues were abolished, and a **uniform system of weights and measures** was adopted.
- Regional dialects were discouraged; **French**, as spoken and written in Paris, became the common language.

The revolutionaries declared it their mission to liberate the peoples of Europe from despotism. Students and members of the educated middle classes set up **Jacobin clubs** in other countries, and the French armies carried the idea of nationalism abroad.

blocks.title: Napoleon: reforms and resentment

blocks.question: Which of these was NOT a feature of the Napoleonic Code of 1804?
options: It gave the vote to all adult men and women
It did away with privileges based on birth
It established equality before the law
It secured the right to property
blocks.explanation: The Napoleonic Code did not give universal suffrage; it denied women rights and made them subject to the authority of fathers and husbands.
option_feedback: This *was* a feature of the Code.
This *was* a feature of the Code.
This *was* a feature of the Code.

sections.title: Europe after Napoleon: liberals and conservatives

blocks.title: A Europe of empires and classes
blocks.body:
In the mid-18th century there were no 'nation-states' as we know them. Germany, Italy and Switzerland were divided into kingdoms, duchies and cantons. Eastern and Central Europe were under autocratic monarchies with many peoples. The **Habsburg Empire** (Austria-Hungary) was a patchwork: German-speaking regions like the Alpine Tyrol, Austria and the Sudetenland, and Bohemia; Italian-speaking Lombardy and Venetia; half of Hungary spoke Magyar; Galicia spoke Polish; and there were many Slav peasants (Bohemians, Slovaks, Slovenes, Croats, Roumans).

**Social classes:** a small, landed **aristocracy** (who spoke French and were united by lifestyle and marriage across Europe) dominated a majority of **peasants**. With industrialisation (England from the late 18th century; France and the German states in the 19th) a **new middle class** of industrialists, businessmen and professionals grew. Among the educated middle class, ideas of national unity following the abolition of aristocratic privileges gained popularity.

**Economic liberalism:** in the German states there were 39 states with their own currencies, weights and measures; a merchant travelling from Hamburg to Nuremberg had to pass 11 customs barriers. In **1834** a customs union, the **Zollverein**, was formed at the initiative of **Prussia** and joined by most German states. It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two. A network of railways improved mobility. Economic nationalism strengthened the wider nationalist feeling.

blocks.title: Liberalism vs conservatism
blocks.body:
| | Liberalism | Conservatism |
|---|---|---|
| Root idea | *liber* (Latin) = free: freedom for the individual, equality before law | preserve traditional institutions: monarchy, Church, social hierarchy, property, family |
| Government | by consent; constitution and representative (elected) parliament | strong monarchy; change only gradually |
| Economy | freedom of markets; abolition of state-imposed restrictions on movement of goods and capital | accepted modernisation (army, bureaucracy, economy) to strengthen monarchy |
| After 1815 | wanted to unite German/Italian states into nation-states | Congress of Vienna (1815) tried to undo Napoleon's changes |

blocks.title: The Congress of Vienna (1815)
blocks.body:
After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, representatives of the European powers **Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria** met at Vienna. The Congress was hosted by the Austrian Chancellor **Duke Metternich**. The **Treaty of Vienna** aimed to undo most of the changes made during the Napoleonic wars.

The conservative regimes set up after 1815 were **autocratic**: they did not tolerate criticism, imposed censorship on newspapers, books, plays and songs, and suppressed liberal ideas. Even so, the memory of the French Revolution inspired liberals.

**Revolutionaries:** many liberal-nationalists went underground and formed secret societies. **Giuseppe Mazzini**, an Italian revolutionary from Genoa, became a member of the secret society of the **Carbonari**. After a failed revolution in Liguria he was sent into exile in **1831**. He founded **Young Italy** in Marseilles and **Young Europe** in Berne. He believed God intended nations to be the natural units of mankind, so Italy could not remain a patchwork of small states. Metternich described him as *"the most dangerous enemy of our social order"*.

blocks.title: What the Treaty of Vienna did
blocks.body:
| Provision of the Treaty of Vienna (1815) | Purpose |
|---|---|
| The Bourbon dynasty restored to power in France | bring back the old monarchy |
| France lost the territories it had annexed under Napoleon | weaken France |
| States set up on France's borders: Kingdom of the Netherlands (with Belgium) in the north; Genoa added to Piedmont in the south | prevent French expansion |
| Prussia given important new territories on its western frontier; Austria given control of northern Italy | strengthen the conservative powers |
| German Confederation of 39 states (set up by Napoleon) left untouched | |
| In the east, Russia given part of Poland; Prussia a portion of Saxony | |

blocks.question: Who hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1815?
blocks.explanation: The Austrian Chancellor, Duke Metternich, hosted the Congress of Vienna.
option_feedback: Bismarck led German unification in the 1860s.
Mazzini was a revolutionary whom Metternich called a dangerous enemy.
The Congress met after Napoleon's defeat.

blocks.question: What was the Zollverein?
options: A treaty that recognised Greece as independent
A customs union of German states formed in 1834 under Prussia
A secret society of Italian revolutionaries
A parliament that met in Frankfurt in 1848
blocks.explanation: The Zollverein (1834) abolished tariff barriers among German states and reduced currencies from over thirty to two.
option_feedback: That was the Treaty of Constantinople (1832).

blocks.title: Revolutions, culture and hunger
blocks.body:
**1830, France:** the **July Revolution** overthrew the Bourbon kings who had been restored in 1815; a constitutional monarchy was set up with **Louis Philippe** at its head. Metternich remarked, *"When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold."* The July Revolution sparked an uprising in Brussels, and **Belgium broke away** from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

**Greece:** Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the 15th century. The struggle for independence began in **1821**. Nationalists got support from Greeks living in exile and from many West Europeans who admired ancient Greek culture. Poets and artists praised Greece as the cradle of European civilisation; the English poet **Lord Byron** organised funds and went to fight, dying of fever in 1824. The **Treaty of Constantinople (1832)** recognised Greece as an independent nation.

**Culture and the nation (Romanticism):** Romantic artists and poets criticised the glorification of reason and focused instead on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings, to create a sense of a shared collective heritage. The German philosopher **Johann Gottfried Herder** claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people, ***das volk***, through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances.
- **Poland**, partitioned at the end of the 18th century by Russia, Prussia and Austria, kept nationalism alive through music and language. **Karol Kurpinski** celebrated the national struggle through his operas and music, turning folk dances like the *polonaise* and *mazurka* into national symbols. After the Russian occupation, Russian was imposed everywhere; after a failed armed rebellion against Russian rule in **1831**, the clergy used Polish as a weapon of resistance, and using Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle.
- In Germany, the **Grimm brothers** collected folktales, seeing them as an expression of the national spirit.

**Hunger and hardship:** the 1830s were years of great economic hardship: population rise, unemployment, competition from cheap machine-made goods from England, food shortages. In **1845** weavers in **Silesia** revolted against contractors who had drastically reduced payments.

**1848:** food shortages and widespread unemployment brought the people of Paris onto the roads. **Louis Philippe was forced to flee**; a National Assembly proclaimed a **Republic**, granted suffrage to all adult males above 21, and guaranteed the right to work. National workshops were set up to provide employment.

blocks.title: The 1848 revolution of the liberals
blocks.body:
Alongside the revolts of the poor, educated middle classes in Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire demanded constitutionalism with national unification: a nation-state based on parliamentary principles, a constitution, freedom of the press and freedom of association.

**Frankfurt Parliament:** in the German regions, middle-class professionals, businessmen and artisans elected an all-German National Assembly. On **18 May 1848**, **831 elected representatives** took their places in the **Church of St Paul** in Frankfurt. They drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament. When the deputies offered the crown to **Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia**, he **rejected it** and joined other monarchs to oppose the elected assembly. The Parliament was dominated by the middle classes, who resisted the demands of workers and artisans and so lost their support. In the end, troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband.

**Women:** the issue of political rights for women was controversial. Women had formed their own associations and newspapers, but they were **denied suffrage** in the Assembly and could attend only as observers in the visitors' gallery.

**Results:** the 1848 uprisings were suppressed, but the autocratic monarchs realised that revolution could be avoided only by concessions. **Serfdom and bonded labour were abolished** in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia, and the Habsburg rulers granted more autonomy to the Hungarians in **1867**.

blocks.question: Which treaty recognised Greece as an independent nation?
blocks.explanation: The Treaty of Constantinople (1832) recognised Greece as an independent nation.
option_feedback: That ended the First World War.
The Treaty of Vienna restored conservative rule after Napoleon.

blocks.question: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail?
options: The King of Prussia rejected the crown and the middle-class deputies lost the support of workers and artisans
Women won the right to vote and opposed the monarchy
blocks.explanation: Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown and opposed the assembly, and the middle classes resisted workers' demands, so the parliament lost support and was disbanded by troops.

sections.title: The making of Germany, Italy and Britain

blocks.title: Nationalism from above
blocks.body:
After 1848, nationalism moved away from democracy and revolution. Conservatives used nationalist feelings to strengthen state power and gain political control.

**Germany: can the army be the architect of a nation?** Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle-class Germans, who tried to unite the German Confederation in 1848 but were crushed by the monarchy and the military, supported by the large landowners of Prussia (the **Junkers**). **Prussia** then took the lead. Its chief minister, **Otto von Bismarck**, was the architect of this process, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy. **Three wars over seven years**, with **Austria, Denmark and France**, ended in Prussian victory. In **January 1871**, the Prussian king **William I** was proclaimed **German Emperor** in a ceremony at **Versailles**. The new state placed a strong emphasis on modernising the currency, banking, legal and judicial systems.

**Italy unified:** Italy was divided into **seven states**; only **Sardinia-Piedmont** was ruled by an Italian princely house. The north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope, and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain. Even the Italian language had many regional variations. Mazzini's revolutionary uprisings of 1831 and 1848 failed. Then **King Victor Emmanuel II** of Sardinia-Piedmont took up the task through war. His chief minister **Count Camillo de Cavour** was neither a revolutionary nor a democrat; like many educated Italians he spoke French much better than Italian. Through a tactful diplomatic alliance with **France**, Sardinia-Piedmont defeated the Austrian forces in **1859**. A large number of armed volunteers under **Giuseppe Garibaldi** joined. In **1860** they marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and drove out the Spanish rulers. In **1861** Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed **king of united Italy**. Most of the people, many of them illiterate peasants, were not aware of the liberal-nationalist ideology.

**The strange case of Britain:** in Britain the nation-state was **not the result of a sudden upheaval or revolution, but of a long-drawn-out process**. Before the 18th century there was no British nation; the English, Welsh, Scots and Irish had their own cultures. The **English** grew in wealth and power and extended their influence. The English **Parliament**, which had seized power from the monarchy in **1688**, was the instrument of nation-building. The **Act of Union (1707)** between England and Scotland created the **United Kingdom of Great Britain**, which in effect meant England imposed its influence on Scotland; Scottish culture and the Gaelic language were suppressed. In **Ireland**, Catholics and Protestants were divided; after a failed revolt led by **Wolfe Tone** and his United Irishmen (1798), Ireland was **forcibly incorporated in 1801**. A new British nation was forged through an English culture: the **British flag (Union Jack)**, the national anthem (**God Save Our Noble King**) and the **English language** were actively promoted.

blocks.title: Germany and Italy compared
blocks.body:
| | Germany | Italy |
|---|---|---|
| Before unity | 39 states in the German Confederation | 7 states; only Sardinia-Piedmont ruled by an Italian princely house |
| Leader state | Prussia | Sardinia-Piedmont |
| Key people | Otto von Bismarck (chief minister), William I | Mazzini, Cavour (chief minister), Garibaldi, Victor Emmanuel II |
| Method | three wars over seven years, with Denmark, Austria and France; army and bureaucracy | diplomacy (alliance with France), war with Austria (1859), Garibaldi's volunteers in the south (1860) |
| Result | January 1871: William I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles | 1861: Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed king of united Italy |

blocks.question: Who was the chief minister of Sardinia-Piedmont who led the movement to unify Italy through diplomacy?
blocks.explanation: Cavour, chief minister of Sardinia-Piedmont, made the alliance with France that defeated Austria in 1859.
option_feedback: Mazzini was a revolutionary in exile.
Garibaldi led armed volunteers; he was not chief minister.
Bismarck was the chief minister of Prussia.

blocks.question: Which statement about the British nation-state is correct?
options: It was created by Bismarck's three wars
Scotland's culture was given equal importance
It developed through a long-drawn-out process, not a sudden revolution
blocks.explanation: Britain's nation-state grew gradually, through the English Parliament, the Act of Union (1707) and the incorporation of Ireland (1801).
option_feedback: Scottish culture and Gaelic were suppressed.

sections.title: Visualising the nation, and the road to war

blocks.title: Nations as women: allegory
blocks.body:
Artists in the 18th and 19th centuries personified nations, showing a country as if it were a person. Nations were portrayed as **female figures**. The female form did not stand for any real woman; it gave the abstract idea of the nation a concrete form. Such a figure is an **allegory**: an abstract idea (greed, envy, freedom, liberty) expressed through a person or a thing.

- **Marianne (France):** a popular Christian name, chosen to underline the idea of a people's nation. Her characteristics were drawn from those of Liberty and the Republic: **the red cap, the tricolour, the cockade**. Statues of Marianne were put up in public squares, and her image was marked on coins and stamps.
- **Germania (Germany):** she wears a **crown of oak leaves**, because the German oak stands for heroism. The painter **Philip Veit** painted Germania in 1848; it hung from the ceiling of St Paul's Church, where the Frankfurt Parliament met.

blocks.title: The symbols around Germania
blocks.body:
| Symbol (Germania, painted by Philip Veit, 1848) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Broken chains | being freed |
| Breastplate with eagle | symbol of the German empire: strength |
| Crown of oak leaves | heroism |
| Sword | readiness to fight |
| Olive branch around the sword | willingness to make peace |
| Black, red and gold tricolour | flag of the liberal-nationalists in 1848, banned by the dukes of the German states |
| Rays of the rising sun | beginning of a new era |

blocks.title: Nationalism and imperialism: the Balkans
blocks.body:
By the last quarter of the 19th century, nationalism no longer kept its idealistic, liberal-democratic spirit. It became a narrow creed with limited ends, and nationalist groups became intolerant of each other and ready to go to war.

The most serious source of tension after 1871 was the **Balkans**, a region of geographical and ethnic variation: modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro. Its inhabitants were broadly known as the **Slavs**. A large part of the Balkans was under the control of the **Ottoman Empire**. The spread of romantic nationalism together with the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made the region very explosive.

- Balkan peoples claimed independence on the basis of nationality, using history to prove they had once been free.
- The Balkan states were jealous of each other and each wanted more territory at the others' expense.
- The great European powers, **Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary**, competed for trade, colonies and naval and military might, and each tried to counter the others' hold over the Balkans.

This led to a series of wars in the region and finally the **First World War (1914)**. Many countries colonised by the Europeans later opposed imperial domination; their anti-imperial movements were nationalist too, but they built their own forms of nationalism.

blocks.question: In the allegory of Germania, what does the crown of oak leaves stand for?
blocks.explanation: The German oak stands for heroism.

blocks.question: Why was the Balkan region called a source of tension after 1871?
options: It had already united peacefully under one king
Rising nationalism, the breakup of the Ottoman Empire and rivalry among the big European powers
It was the home of the Frankfurt Parliament
blocks.explanation: Slav nationalism, Ottoman decline and great-power rivalry made the Balkans explosive and led to the First World War.
option_feedback: The Balkan states were rivals, not united.
Most of it was under the Ottoman Empire.
The Frankfurt Parliament met in Germany.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **French collective identity, "P-C-T-N-H-C-W-L":** **P**atrie, **C**itoyen, **T**ricolour, **N**ational Assembly, **H**ymns/oaths, **C**entralised laws, **W**eights and measures, **L**anguage (French).
- **Germany = B-P-W-3-71:** **B**ismarck, **P**russia, **W**illiam I, **3** wars (Denmark, Austria, France: *DAF*), **1871**.
- **Italy = M-C-G-V:** **M**azzini (heart), **C**avour (brain), **G**aribaldi (sword), **V**ictor Emmanuel II (crown). 1859 → 1860 → 1861.
- **Treaty of Vienna = undo Napoleon:** Bourbons back, buffer states round France, gifts to Prussia, Austria and Russia.
- **Germania's symbols:** "Chains broken, Eagle strong, Oak brave, Sword ready, Olive peaceful, Sun new."

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying the Napoleonic Code gave women equal rights: it did not.
2. Mixing up Metternich (Austria, Congress of Vienna) and Bismarck (Prussia, German unification).
3. Writing that the Frankfurt Parliament made Friedrich Wilhelm IV emperor: he **rejected** the crown.
4. Saying Garibaldi was king of Italy: Victor Emmanuel II became king in 1861.
5. Saying Britain was formed by revolution: it was a long process.
6. Confusing the Treaty of Vienna (1815) with the Treaty of Constantinople (1832).
7. Writing *Zollverein* as a political party: it was a customs union.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Show Sorrieu's print and Veit's Germania and let students find the symbols themselves before revealing the meanings. Then split the class into three groups (Germany, Italy, Britain); each group explains its nation's making in two minutes, and the class votes on which path was most democratic.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Was the unification of Germany a victory for the people's nationalism of 1848 or for the Prussian state? Give one reason for your view.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 2, Nationalism in India:** Indian nationalism grew through anti-colonial struggle; compare it with the European paths.
- **Political Science, Power Sharing and Federalism:** how modern nations hold diverse peoples together.
- **Bharat Mata** (painted by Abanindranath Tagore) is India's allegory, like Marianne and Germania.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
In 120 words, compare the unification of Italy with the unification of Germany under: leaders, method and result.

**Model answer:** Both were divided into many states and unified under the leadership of one kingdom. In Germany, Prussia's chief minister Otto von Bismarck used the army and bureaucracy in three wars (with Denmark, Austria and France); in January 1871 William I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles. In Italy, Sardinia-Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II and his chief minister Cavour used diplomacy and an alliance with France to defeat Austria (1859), while Garibaldi's volunteers freed the south (1860); Victor Emmanuel II became king of united Italy in 1861. Germany's unification was mainly by military power from above; Italy's combined diplomacy, war and popular volunteers.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- The French Revolution (1789) made the people the nation; collective identity was built through symbols, laws, language and uniform measures.
- Napoleon's Civil Code (1804) ended birth privileges and gave equality before law, but taxes, censorship and conscription caused resentment.
- The new middle class supported liberal nationalism; economic unity came through the Zollverein (1834).
- The Congress of Vienna (1815, Metternich) restored conservative rule; secret societies and Mazzini kept the idea of nation alive.
- 1830–1848: July Revolution, Belgian and Greek independence, Romanticism (Herder, Polish music and language), hunger revolts, the 1848 revolution and the failed Frankfurt Parliament.
- Germany was unified by Bismarck and Prussia (1871), Italy by Cavour, Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel II (1861); Britain grew by a long process.
- Nations were shown as women (Marianne, Germania). Narrow nationalism and imperial rivalry in the Balkans led to the First World War.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- 5-mark questions often ask: Treaty of Vienna provisions, Britain's long process, German unification, steps of the French revolutionaries, Napoleon's reforms, the 1848 liberals.
- Write points with names and dates (1804, 1815, 1832, 1834, 1848, 1861, 1871).
- In MCQs on pictures (Sorrieu, Germania), learn the symbol table.
- Assertion-reason questions test cause and effect: check both statements separately first.

blocks.back: Abolished tariff barriers among German states and reduced currencies from over 30 to 2.

When and where was William I proclaimed German Emperor?
